clinicalPearls: Presents characteristically as a malignant effusion in the pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal cavity without a discrete tumour mass
Universally associated with human herpesvirus 8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus), and frequently co-infected with Epstein-Barr virus
Occurs predominantly in the context of immunodeficiency, especially advanced HIV infection, and may coexist with Kaposi sarcoma or multicentric Castleman disease
Malignant cells have a large, anaplastic or immunoblastic/plasmablastic appearance and a distinctive null or aberrant immunophenotype
Cells typically lack pan-B-cell markers such as CD20 but express activation and plasma-cell-associated markers like CD30, CD38, and CD138, with HHV-8 latent nuclear antigen detectable in the nuclei
A rare extracavitary/solid variant can form masses in lymph nodes or extranodal sites while retaining the same viral and immunophenotypic features
Diagnosis rests on cytology of the effusion combined with HHV-8 demonstration
reference.pathophysiology: Primary effusion lymphoma is a large B-cell neoplasm driven by human herpesvirus 8, which encodes latent proteins that dysregulate the cell cycle, inhibit apoptosis, and promote proliferation of infected B-cells. Most tumours also harbour Epstein-Barr virus, which is thought to cooperate in transformation. The malignant cells have undergone extensive plasmacytic differentiation, explaining loss of typical B-cell antigens and gain of plasma-cell markers. They proliferate preferentially within serous body cavities, producing lymphomatous effusions rather than solid masses, and the underlying immunodeficiency permits unchecked viral-driven expansion.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive or infective effusions in immunocompromised patients
Malignant effusion from carcinoma or mesothelioma
HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease with effusions
additionalInvestigations: Cytological examination of effusion fluid with cell block preparation
Immunophenotyping showing loss of CD20 with expression of CD30, CD38, CD138
Detection of HHV-8 latent nuclear antigen by immunohistochemistry and HHV-8 by molecular methods
In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA
HIV testing and assessment of immune status
Cross-sectional imaging to identify effusions, exclude solid masses, and detect Kaposi sarcoma or Castleman disease
redFlags: Large pericardial effusion causing tamponade physiology
Respiratory compromise from a massive pleural effusion
Rapid reaccumulation of effusion after drainage
Concurrent opportunistic infection in the immunodeficient host
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor with short median survival, though outcomes improve with combination chemotherapy alongside effective antiretroviral therapy and control of the underlying immunodeficiency.
pitfalls: Dismissing a malignant effusion as reactive because no mass is seen on imaging
Missing the diagnosis by not testing effusion cells for HHV-8
Being misled by loss of CD20 into excluding a B-cell lymphoma
Neglecting optimisation of antiretroviral therapy and immune reconstitution
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
